option_description: Controls whether role definitions grant only the minimum permissions required for each role's stated function, or whether permissions are broader and potentially excessive. This attribute captures the overall philosophy and implementation quality of least-privilege design across all defined roles.
security_impact: Directly gates the least_privilege_enforcement countermeasure. The Rego policy requires role_permission_scope to be 'minimal' or 'appropriate' (never 'excessive') as a prerequisite for the countermeasure to activate. Excessive permissions increase blast radius when accounts are compromised, enabling attackers to access resources far beyond the intended scope of a given role.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For AWS IAM, enumerate all IAM policies attached to roles and evaluate action scope. Look for broad action patterns such as 's3:*', 'ec2:*', or 'iam:*' that exceed the stated role function.
how_to_obtain.command: aws iam list-roles --query 'Roles[*].RoleName' --output text | tr '\t' '\n' | xargs -I {} sh -c 'echo "=== {} ==="; aws iam list-role-policies --role-name {} --output text; aws iam list-attached-role-policies --role-name {} --query "AttachedPolicies[*].PolicyName" --output text'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A list of roles with their inline and attached policy names. Flag roles where policy names suggest broad access (e.g., AdministratorAccess, PowerUserAccess) for deeper permission review.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query your application's RBAC configuration API or database to retrieve role-to-permission mappings and compare each role's permission set against its documented job function description.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN' https://<app-host>/api/v1/roles?include=permissions | jq '.roles[] | {name: .name, permission_count: (.permissions | length), permissions: .permissions}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON listing each role with its assigned permissions. Roles with permission counts significantly higher than peer roles or containing action categories unrelated to their stated function indicate 'excessive' scope.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect application role configuration files (e.g., Casbin policy files, Rails ability definitions, Spring Security role configs) for permission breadth and compare against documented role descriptions.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any lines matching wildcard or catch-all patterns indicate potentially excessive scope. Zero matches suggest role definitions are action-specific.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the IAM or access management console and review each role's permission summary. Most cloud and enterprise IAM UIs display a permission summary with breadth indicators or 'admin-equivalent' warnings.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Console: IAM > Roles > [Role Name] > Permissions tab > Review each policy's JSON for action patterns | Azure Portal: Azure Active Directory > App Registrations > [App] > API Permissions | Okta Admin: Security > API > Authorization Servers > [Server] > Scopes
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Role permission summaries showing specific, function-aligned action lists. Roles flagged as 'Provides full access' or similar indicate excessive scope.

option_description: Indicates whether any role definition contains wildcard or catch-all permission entries such as '*', 'admin:*', 'iam:*', or equivalent broad action groups that bypass the specificity requirement of least-privilege design. A single wildcard entry in any role triggers this flag as true.
security_impact: Used as a hard-negative condition in the least_privilege_enforcement Rego rule — both evaluation paths require wildcard_permissions_present == false for the countermeasure to activate. Wildcard permissions mean a role can perform any action within a resource domain, regardless of functional need, creating extreme privilege escalation risk if the role is assigned to a compromised account or misused.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Scan all IAM policy documents for wildcard action entries across inline and managed policies. This covers AWS IAM but the pattern applies to any JSON-based policy store.
how_to_obtain.command: aws iam list-policies --scope Local --query 'Policies[*].Arn' --output text | tr '\t' '\n' | xargs -I {} sh -c 'VERSION=$(aws iam get-policy --policy-arn {} --query Policy.DefaultVersionId --output text); aws iam get-policy-version --policy-arn {} --version-id $VERSION --query PolicyVersion.Document' | python3 -c "import json,sys; data=sys.stdin.read(); [print(f'WILDCARD FOUND: {s}') for s in __import__('re').findall(r'\"Action\":\s*\"[^\"]*\*[^\"]*\"', data)]"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines prefixed with 'WILDCARD FOUND:' listing each wildcard action string. No output indicates wildcard_permissions_present should be set to false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search application RBAC configuration files, Kubernetes RBAC manifests, or OPA/Rego policy files for wildcard verb or resource entries.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: File paths and line numbers where wildcard entries exist. No output means no wildcards detected. Each hit should be reviewed to determine if the wildcard is intentional (e.g., superadmin role) and documented.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the application or cloud provider API to retrieve all permission definitions and programmatically test for wildcard pattern presence.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN' https://<app-host>/api/v1/permissions | jq '[.permissions[] | select(.action | test("\\*|:all$|^all$"))] | if length > 0 then {wildcard_found: true, entries: .} else {wildcard_found: false} end'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response with wildcard_found: false and an empty entries array when no wildcard permissions exist. Any truthy result requires remediation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the cloud console's built-in policy analyzer or permission viewer to identify overly permissive policies. AWS IAM Access Analyzer and Azure Policy Compliance both highlight wildcard permission issues.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Console: IAM > Policies > [Policy] > JSON tab > search for ':*' or '"*"' entries | AWS IAM Access Analyzer: Access Analyzer > Findings > filter by 'Policy type: Identity' | Azure Portal: Policy > Compliance > filter for 'Wildcard permissions' built-in definitions
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Policy JSON viewer shows only specific action names (e.g., 's3:GetObject') with no wildcard entries. Access Analyzer shows zero findings related to overly permissive policies.

option_description: Captures how frequently role-permission assignments are reviewed and recertified to ensure they remain compliant with least-privilege requirements. Options range from continuous automated validation through quarterly and annual manual reviews to no review process at all.
security_impact: Used in the second evaluation path of the least_privilege_enforcement Rego rule, which requires privilege_review_frequency to be 'continuous' or 'quarterly' alongside minimal scope, SoD enforcement, and no wildcards. Infrequent or absent reviews allow permission drift — roles accumulate unnecessary permissions over time as features are added without corresponding privilege reviews, leaving the environment perpetually over-privileged.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review access management policy documentation and recertification campaign schedules to identify the formally documented review cadence. Request the last three access review completion reports to confirm the schedule is actually followed.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Request from IAM team: access management policy document, access recertification campaign schedule, last three campaign completion reports with dates and coverage metrics
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documentation explicitly stating review frequency (e.g., 'quarterly' = every 90 days). Completion reports should show review dates within the stated cadence with >90% completion rates.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check identity governance platforms for configured recertification campaign schedules. Tools like SailPoint, Saviynt, or Microsoft Entra ID Governance maintain campaign history and schedules.
how_to_obtain.navigation: SailPoint IdentityIQ: Governance > Certifications > Campaigns > Active/Scheduled | Saviynt: Access Governance > Certifications > Campaign Schedule | Microsoft Entra ID: Identity Governance > Access Reviews > All Reviews (filter by status and date)
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A list of scheduled or completed campaigns with their frequency configuration (e.g., 'Recurs every 90 days'). Absence of any campaigns maps to 'never'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query AWS IAM Access Advisor or equivalent tooling to determine when last access review activity occurred and whether automated drift detection is configured.
how_to_obtain.command: aws iam generate-service-last-accessed-details --arn $(aws iam list-roles --query 'Roles[0].Arn' --output text) --query '{JobId: JobId}' --output text | xargs -I {} aws iam get-service-last-accessed-details --job-id {} --query 'ServicesLastAccessed[*].{ServiceName: ServiceName, LastAuth: LastAuthenticated}' --output table
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Table showing last authentication dates per service. Combined with automated review tooling, continuous access review means near-real-time visibility into unused permissions. Long gaps (>90 days) between last access and today suggest infrequent review.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query your IAM governance API or SIEM for access review job scheduling configuration to confirm programmatic review cadence.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN' https://<governance-platform>/api/v1/access-reviews/schedule | jq '{frequency: .schedule.frequency, last_run: .last_execution.completed_at, next_run: .next_execution.scheduled_at, automated: .automated_detection_enabled}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON object showing frequency field mapping to one of: 'continuous', 'quarterly', 'annually'. The automated field indicates whether drift detection supplements manual campaigns.

option_description: Controls whether the RBAC model actively prevents any single role from combining mutually exclusive high-privilege permissions — for example, preventing a single role from holding both 'create financial transaction' and 'approve financial transaction' permissions simultaneously.
security_impact: Required as true in both evaluation paths of the least_privilege_enforcement Rego rule. Without SoD enforcement, a single compromised or malicious account can complete sensitive multi-step workflows end-to-end without any second-party check, enabling fraud, unauthorized data modification, and undetected privilege abuse. SoD is also a core requirement of SOX, PCI-DSS, and ISO 27001 compliance frameworks.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review RBAC policy documents, IAM permission boundary configurations, or application role constraint definitions for documented SoD constraint rules that explicitly prevent conflicting permission combinations.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Configuration blocks showing SoD constraint definitions, such as 'conflicting_roles: [approver, executor]' or 'sod_constraints: [{role_a: creator, role_b: approver, action: deny_if_same_user}]'. No results indicate SoD is not configured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the IAM or application security team to understand whether SoD constraints exist as preventive controls in the RBAC system or only as detective controls in audit logging.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Request: SoD constraint matrix (list of conflicting role pairs), evidence of enforcement mechanism (preventive blocking vs. alerting only), last SoD violation report, and any exceptions approved by risk management
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A documented SoD matrix showing role pairs that cannot be co-assigned to a user, with evidence that the RBAC system rejects assignment attempts that violate these constraints (preventive), not merely reports them after the fact.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt to assign conflicting roles to a test user account in a non-production environment to verify the RBAC system actively rejects SoD-violating assignments.
how_to_obtain.command:
# Test SoD enforcement by attempting conflicting role assignment (non-production only)
curl -s -X POST -H 'Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"user_id": "test-sod-user", "role": "approver"}' https://<app-host>/api/v1/users/test-sod-user/roles | jq .; curl -s -X POST -H 'Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"user_id": "test-sod-user", "role": "creator"}' https://<app-host>/api/v1/users/test-sod-user/roles | jq '{status: .status, error: .error}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The second role assignment call should return HTTP 409 Conflict or HTTP 403 Forbidden with an error message referencing SoD constraint violation. A 200 OK response indicates SoD is NOT enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check IAM governance or IGA platform for configured SoD policy rulesets. Platforms like SailPoint, Oracle Identity Governance, and Saviynt provide SoD policy management with violation reporting.
how_to_obtain.navigation: SailPoint IIQ: Governance > Policy Management > Separation of Duties Policies | Oracle OIG: Compliance > Segregation of Duties > Policy List | Saviynt: Security Manager > SOD > Policy Rules | Microsoft Entra ID Governance: Entitlement Management > Access Packages > Incompatible Access Packages
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A list of active SoD policies showing conflicting role pairs with enforcement mode set to 'Preventive' (blocks assignment) rather than 'Detective' (only reports violations after assignment).

option_description: Records the current number of users who have been assigned to roles that grant permissions exceeding their documented job function requirements, as determined by access reviews, automated privilege analytics, or recertification campaigns. This is a point-in-time count of known over-privileged accounts.
security_impact: Serves as contextual evidence in the least_privilege_enforcement rule evaluation. A non-zero count demonstrates that even if role definitions are well-scoped, the actual user population has drifted away from least-privilege compliance. Each over-privileged user represents an expanded attack surface — a compromised credential has access to resources and actions far beyond the user's legitimate need, amplifying potential breach impact.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use AWS IAM Access Analyzer or equivalent tooling to identify users with unused permissions, which is a strong proxy for over-privileged accounts. Count distinct users with significant unused permission sets.
how_to_obtain.command:
aws iam get-account-authorization-details --filter User --query 'UserDetailList[*].[UserName,AttachedManagedPolicies[*].PolicyName,UserPolicyList[*].PolicyName]' --output json | python3 -c "
import json, sys, subprocess
users = json.load(sys.stdin)
over_priv = []
for u in users:
    result = subprocess.run(['aws','iam','generate-service-last-accessed-details','--arn', f'arn:aws:iam::$(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text):user/{u[0]}'], capture_output=True, text=True)
    over_priv.append(u[0])
print(f'Users requiring review: {len(over_priv)}')
"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A count of users with assigned permissions that exceed their last-accessed service footprint. The definitive over-privileged count should come from a completed access review where reviewers explicitly flagged excess roles.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query your IGA or PAM platform's over-privileged user report endpoint, which compares assigned roles against job function profiles or peer group analysis.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN' 'https://<iga-platform>/api/v2/reports/over-privileged-users?status=active&include_count=true' | jq '{total_over_privileged: .summary.count, users: [.users[] | {username: .username, excess_roles: .excess_role_count, last_reviewed: .last_review_date}]} '
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response with total_over_privileged as an integer. Zero indicates full compliance. Any positive value should trigger remediation action. Expect the platform to provide per-user detail of which specific roles are flagged as excess.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Pull the most recent access recertification campaign results from your IGA platform or audit log system. Count users whose manager or access owner clicked 'Revoke' during review, indicating confirmed excess access.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An integer count of unique users whose access was flagged for revocation in the most recent review cycle. This is the most reliable source for over_privileged_user_count as it reflects human manager judgment.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Access your identity governance platform's analytics dashboard to retrieve the current over-privileged user count from the most recently completed access review or continuous monitoring feed.
how_to_obtain.navigation: SailPoint IdentityIQ: Dashboard > Access Review Results > Revoked Items > count distinct users | Saviynt: Analytics > Over-Privileged Users > Current Count widget | Microsoft Entra ID Governance: Access Reviews > [Review Name] > Results > filter 'Decision: Deny' > count | AWS IAM: Access Analyzer > Findings > filter 'Finding type: Unused access'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A numeric count displayed in the dashboard widget or report summary. Zero over-privileged users in a large organization often indicates the review process was not thorough. Typical organizations identify 5-15% of users as over-privileged during first-time reviews.

option_description: Indicates whether the organization has a formal, documented periodic process for validating that user-to-role assignments remain aligned with current job responsibilities. This includes scheduled recertification campaigns, automated drift detection workflows, or structured manager review procedures.
security_impact: Required as true in both evaluation paths of the role_assignment_accuracy Rego rule. Without a formal review process, role assignments accumulate over time as users change positions, take on temporary projects, or leave the organization — resulting in persistent orphaned and excess permissions. The countermeasure cannot activate if this is false, regardless of how frequently reviews happen.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request the access management policy document and evidence of the most recently completed role review campaign. Verify the process is formally documented with defined ownership, scope, and completion criteria.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Request from IAM/GRC team: access management or IAM policy document (version-controlled, approved by CISO or equivalent), access recertification procedure document, campaign completion report from the last cycle showing reviewer names, dates, and completion percentage
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A formal policy document containing a section on access reviews with defined frequency, responsible parties, and escalation procedures. Combined with at least one completed campaign report, this confirms the process exists and is operational.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check whether access review campaigns are configured in the identity governance platform, which confirms the process is operationalized rather than just documented.
how_to_obtain.navigation: SailPoint IdentityIQ: Governance > Certifications > Campaigns > Active or Scheduled | Microsoft Entra ID: Identity Governance > Access Reviews > New Access Review (check for existing templates and history) | Saviynt: Access Governance > Certifications > Campaign list | Sailpoint IdentityNow: Access Reviews > Campaigns
how_to_obtain.expected_output: At least one configured campaign template or scheduled campaign with defined reviewers, scope, and frequency. The presence of completed historical campaigns confirms the process has been executed, not just planned.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search the audit log system for access review completion events, which confirm a review process was executed within the organization's stated frequency.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Log entries showing access review completion events with timestamps. Any matching entries confirm the process exists and has been executed. No entries across 12 months of logs indicates the process does not exist or is not being run.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the IGA or ITSM platform's campaign history API to confirm access review campaigns have been created and completed.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN' 'https://<iga-platform>/api/v1/access-reviews/history?limit=5&sort=completed_at:desc' | jq '{process_exists: (. | length > 0), recent_campaigns: [.[] | {name: .name, completed: .completed_at, completion_rate: .completion_percentage}]}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response with process_exists: true and at least one entry in recent_campaigns with a valid completed date. An empty array or 404 response confirms no formal process exists.

option_description: Specifies the maximum number of days permitted between consecutive role assignment reviews. This is the policy-configured or operationally observed cadence — for example, 90 days for quarterly reviews, 180 days for semi-annual, or 365 days for annual cycles. Valid values range from 1 to 730 days.
security_impact: Evaluated in both paths of the role_assignment_accuracy Rego rule. The first path requires ≤90 days (quarterly), and the second path requires ≤180 days (semi-annual) — both activate the countermeasure when combined with role_review_process_exists == true and orphaned_role_assignments_remediated == true. Reviews occurring less than twice yearly allow permission drift to persist for extended periods, increasing the window of exposure from orphaned and accumulated role assignments.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the access management policy or IAM governance standard to find the formally mandated maximum days between access reviews. Cross-reference against actual campaign dates to confirm policy is being followed.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Request: IAM governance policy document (search for 'access review frequency', 'recertification period', 'review cycle'), last three campaign completion dates to calculate actual intervals, any exception approvals extending the standard cycle
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Policy document stating a specific maximum review interval in days or as a named frequency (quarterly = 90 days, semi-annual = 180 days, annual = 365 days). Actual campaign dates should align within ±15 days of the stated interval.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the configured recurrence schedule on access review campaigns in the IGA platform, which reflects the operationalized review frequency.
how_to_obtain.navigation: SailPoint IdentityIQ: Governance > Certifications > Campaigns > [Campaign] > Schedule > Recurrence interval (displayed in days or as frequency label) | Microsoft Entra ID: Identity Governance > Access Reviews > [Review] > Settings > Recurrence > Duration and Frequency | Saviynt: Access Governance > Certifications > [Campaign] > Schedule > Frequency
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A numeric recurrence interval displayed in the campaign settings. Convert named frequencies: Daily=1, Weekly=7, Monthly=30, Quarterly=90, Semi-Annual=180, Annual=365. This is the authoritative source for the configured review_frequency_days value.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Calculate actual review intervals from audit log timestamps to determine the real-world frequency regardless of what policy documents state.
how_to_obtain.command: grep 'access_review_completed\|certification_completed' /var/log/iam/audit.log | awk '{print $1, $2}' | sort | awk 'NR>1{cmd="date -d \"" $0 "\" +%s"; cmd | getline ts; close(cmd); diff=ts-prev; print "Days between reviews:", diff/86400} {cmd="date -d \"" $0 "\" +%s"; cmd | getline prev; close(cmd)}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A series of 'Days between reviews: N' lines showing the actual cadence. Consistent values around 90 indicate quarterly reviews. Values over 180 suggest semi-annual or worse. Inconsistent values indicate an ad-hoc process.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the governance platform API for campaign schedule configuration to retrieve the numeric frequency value directly.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN' 'https://<iga-platform>/api/v1/access-reviews/schedule/active' | jq '{frequency_days: .recurrence_interval_days, frequency_label: .recurrence_label, next_due: .next_scheduled_date, last_completed: .last_completion_date}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON with frequency_days as an integer between 1 and 730. A value of 90 or less satisfies the first Rego path; 180 or less satisfies the second path. Values above 365 represent high risk from permission drift.

option_description: Indicates whether a confirmed, operational process or automated control exists to detect and remove role assignments belonging to users who are no longer active — including terminated employees, contractors who have ended engagements, or users who have transferred to different roles or departments. This requires both detection and timely remediation capabilities.
security_impact: Required as true in both evaluation paths of the role_assignment_accuracy Rego rule — no combination of review process and frequency satisfies the countermeasure without this control. Orphaned role assignments are among the highest-risk access control failures because former employees or contractors may retain working credentials with active permissions long after their legitimate access need ends, creating persistent insider threat and credential abuse vectors.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify integration between HR offboarding workflows and IAM/RBAC systems. Request evidence of the deprovisioning workflow, including automated triggers, SLA for role removal, and exception handling procedures.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Request from HR and IAM teams: offboarding workflow documentation showing the step where IAM/RBAC access revocation is triggered, average time-to-revoke metric from last quarter, list of deprovisioning exceptions with approved grace periods, HR-to-IAM system integration architecture diagram
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documented workflow with an explicit IAM revocation step triggered within 24 hours of termination/transfer event. Automated triggers (HR system webhook, SCIM provisioning event, or scheduled reconciliation) confirm remediation is systemic rather than manual.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Reconcile active role assignments against current HR records to identify orphaned accounts. Compare RBAC user lists against the authoritative HR/directory system.
how_to_obtain.command:
# Compare active RBAC users against HR-sourced active employee list
comm -23 \
  <(curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN' https://<app-host>/api/v1/users?status=active | jq -r '.users[].username' | sort) \
  <(ldapsearch -x -H ldap://<ldap-host> -D 'cn=svc-audit,dc=corp,dc=com' -w $LDAP_PASS -b 'ou=employees,dc=corp,dc=com' '(employeeStatus=active)' uid | grep '^uid:' | awk '{print $2}' | sort) \
| head -20
echo "Orphaned account count: $(comm -23 <(...) <(...) | wc -l)"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: List of usernames present in RBAC but absent from active HR records. Zero results confirm orphaned_role_assignments_remediated should be true. Any results indicate active orphaned assignments requiring immediate remediation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for automated deprovisioning workflows in your IGA or IAM platform that are triggered by HR events, and review the orphaned account detection report.
how_to_obtain.navigation: SailPoint IdentityIQ: Life Cycle Manager > Leaver Workflows > Active workflows showing 'Terminate Identity' steps | Microsoft Entra ID: Identity Governance > Lifecycle Workflows > Leaver workflows | Saviynt: Lifecycle Management > Joiners-Movers-Leavers > Leaver workflow status | Okta Workflows: Flows > search 'offboarding' or 'deprovisioning' for active flow definitions
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An active, enabled leaver/offboarding workflow with an explicit role revocation step and a trigger connected to HR system events. The workflow execution history should show recent successful completions corresponding to known termination events.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check SCIM provisioning logs or HR-to-IAM sync logs for deprovisioning events to confirm the automated remediation process is executing successfully.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Recent successful deprovisioning events with timestamps. The presence of entries within the past 30 days (assuming regular turnover) confirms the automated process is operational. Absence of any deprovisioning events in an organization with employee turnover indicates the process is not functioning.

option_description: Controls whether role-based access control gates are applied to all application actions, only some, or none. This determines the breadth of the RBAC policy across every route, controller method, and API endpoint in the application.
security_impact: This attribute is a direct condition in the permission_boundary_coverage Rego rule: the policy only activates when rbac_enforcement_scope == 'all_actions'. A value of 'partial' or 'none' means the countermeasure fails entirely, leaving unprotected endpoints exploitable by unauthenticated or under-privileged users. Full enforcement scope is the foundation upon which all other RBAC controls depend.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Enumerate all registered routes and check for attached authorization middleware in a Node.js/Express application by scanning route definitions for missing auth guards.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any lines returned indicate unprotected routes, suggesting 'partial' or 'none'. Zero results indicate 'all_actions'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Spring Boot applications, list all @RequestMapping/@GetMapping/@PostMapping endpoints and verify each has @PreAuthorize or @Secured annotations.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Files listed lack method-level security annotations, indicating partial or missing RBAC enforcement.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the global security configuration or middleware pipeline definition to determine if a blanket authorization filter is applied before all routes.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A global middleware entry covering all route groups indicates 'all_actions'; route-specific entries suggest 'partial'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In an API gateway such as AWS API Gateway or Kong, navigate to the Routes or Services list and inspect each endpoint's authorization plugins/policies to identify any without an auth enforcer.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Console → API Gateway → Select API → Resources → Select Method → Method Request → Authorization. Kong Manager → Services → Select Service → Routes → Plugins tab.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Every method showing a configured authorizer or plugin indicates 'all_actions'; any showing 'NONE' indicates at minimum 'partial'.

option_description: Represents the exact number of application routes, controller actions, or API endpoints that can be invoked without passing through any role-based access control check. A value of 0 means full RBAC coverage.
security_impact: The permission_boundary_coverage Rego rule requires unprotected_action_count == 0 in conjunction with rbac_enforcement_scope == 'all_actions'. Even a single unprotected endpoint can be exploited for unauthorized data access or privilege escalation. This count provides a precise, measurable gap metric for remediation prioritization.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use a static analysis script to count endpoints lacking authorization decorators in a Python Django application.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Integer count of view functions without auth decorators. Target value is 0.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Laravel PHP applications, extract all registered routes and identify those with no middleware assignment containing 'auth' or a role gate.
how_to_obtain.command: php artisan route:list --json | python3 -c "import json,sys; routes=json.load(sys.stdin); print(sum(1 for r in routes if not any('auth' in str(m) for m in r.get('middleware',[]))))"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A non-zero integer indicates the count of unprotected routes. Zero confirms full coverage.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the application's OpenAPI/Swagger specification to count paths that lack a security scheme definition.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s http://localhost:8080/v3/api-docs | python3 -c "import json,sys; spec=json.load(sys.stdin); paths=spec.get('paths',{}); print(sum(1 for p in paths.values() for m in p.values() if isinstance(m,dict) and 'security' not in m))"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Returns integer count of operations without a security requirement object. Target is 0.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request the development team's route-to-permission mapping spreadsheet or access control matrix and count rows where the 'Required Role' column is empty or marked 'Public'.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Request document from application security team or development lead. Review columns: Endpoint, HTTP Method, Required Role/Permission.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Count of rows with no role requirement. Ideally 0 outside explicitly public endpoints such as health checks or login pages.

option_description: Determines whether the RBAC engine operates under an implicit-deny posture, meaning any action not explicitly granted by a role assignment is automatically blocked. This is the foundational closed-world assumption for access control.
security_impact: The permission_boundary_coverage Rego rule requires default_deny_policy_enabled == true. Without it, new or unclassified endpoints may be implicitly accessible, and any gap in policy coverage becomes an exploitable hole. Default-deny is the enforcement backstop that makes rbac_enforcement_scope == 'all_actions' meaningful even when policy gaps exist.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the authorization framework configuration for a default effect or fallback setting. For OPA-based systems, look for a default allow rule set to false.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'default allow := false' or 'defaultEffect: Deny' confirms default-deny is enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For AWS IAM-based applications, confirm that no wildcard Allow policy is attached at the resource level that would override explicit denies.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An empty array or only explicitly listed actions indicates default-deny behavior.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Keycloak, navigate to Realm Settings → Authorization → Policies and check the Decision Strategy set on the resource server to confirm 'Unanimous' or 'Affirmative' with an explicit default deny policy.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Keycloak Admin Console → Clients → Select Application Client → Authorization → Settings → Decision Strategy. Also check Authorization → Policies for a Deny policy with POSITIVE logic applied broadly.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Decision Strategy of 'Unanimous' with no catch-all allow policy confirms default-deny posture.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the application architect or security lead to confirm whether the RBAC framework documentation specifies a closed-world or open-world assumption, and request evidence such as policy documents or framework configuration guides.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Request access control design document, architecture decision records (ADRs), or RBAC policy specification from the application team.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Written confirmation that the system blocks all actions unless explicitly permitted, with no implicit allow for unmatched requests.

option_description: Identifies whether any mechanism exists in the application that circumvents RBAC enforcement, including debug flags, hardcoded admin credentials, IP-allowlist-based auth skipping, special query parameters, or disabled authorization middleware.
security_impact: The permission_boundary_coverage Rego rule requires bypass_mechanisms_present == false. Any bypass mechanism, regardless of intent, creates an exploitable attack surface. Debug backdoors left in production are a common source of critical vulnerabilities. Even a single bypass invalidates the assurance provided by all other RBAC controls.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Scan application source code for common bypass patterns including debug flags, skip-auth parameters, and hardcoded admin tokens.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Zero matches confirms no obvious bypass mechanisms. Any match requires manual review to determine if it is reachable in production.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review environment configuration files and deployment manifests for flags that disable authentication or authorization middleware.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No entries, or entries showing AUTH_ENABLED=true and SKIP_AUTHZ=false, indicate no bypass mechanisms in configuration.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for commented-out authorization middleware or guards in routing and controller files.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Commented-out authorization calls indicate previously disabled controls and should be treated as potential bypass mechanisms.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Analyze access logs for requests that reached protected endpoints without any authentication token or session, which may indicate an active bypass.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No 200-status responses to protected paths with missing auth headers confirms no active bypass. Any results require immediate investigation.

option_description: Indicates whether the system has a formal, documented set of mutually exclusive role pairs or role sets that cannot be simultaneously held by a single user, forming the policy foundation for Separation of Duties enforcement.
security_impact: Both separation_of_duties_support Rego rule branches require sod_constraints_defined == true as the mandatory base condition. Without formally defined constraints, the system cannot enforce or detect SoD violations regardless of enforcement mode settings. Undefined SoD constraints mean a single compromised or malicious user could hold both requestor and approver roles, enabling fraud or unauthorized privilege escalation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the RBAC policy configuration or authorization engine for explicit SoD constraint definitions listing incompatible role pairs.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of named constraint entries pairing incompatible roles confirms sod_constraints_defined=true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In SailPoint IdentityIQ or similar IGA platform, navigate to the Policy Management section to view defined Segregation of Duties policies listing role conflicts.
how_to_obtain.navigation: SailPoint IdentityIQ → Governance → Policies → Segregation of Duties. IBM ISIM → Policy → Separation of Duties. Saviynt → Security Manager → Entitlement Conflicts.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A populated list of named SoD policies with defined conflicting role/entitlement pairs confirms constraints are defined.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the identity governance platform's API to retrieve defined SoD policies and confirm at least one active constraint exists.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' 'https://iga-platform.example.com/api/v1/policies/sod' | python3 -c "import json,sys; data=json.load(sys.stdin); print(f'SoD policies defined: {len(data.get(\"policies\", []))}; Active: {sum(1 for p in data.get(\"policies\",[]) if p.get(\"status\")==\"active\")}')"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output showing count > 0 for defined and active policies confirms sod_constraints_defined=true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request the application's role access control matrix or risk matrix from the compliance or IAM team, verifying that incompatible role combinations are explicitly documented.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Request Role Conflict Matrix, SoD Policy Document, or Access Control Matrix from IAM team or compliance officer.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A document listing at minimum pairs such as 'PurchaseRequester/PurchaseApprover' and 'DataEntryClerk/Auditor' as incompatible confirms constraints are defined.

option_description: Specifies how SoD constraints are operationally enforced: 'preventive' means the system actively blocks conflicting role assignments at the point of provisioning; 'detective' means violations are allowed but flagged and reported after the fact; 'none' means no enforcement occurs despite constraints potentially being defined.
security_impact: The separation_of_duties_support Rego rule's strongest path requires sod_enforcement_mode == 'preventive'. The second path accepts 'detective' only when dual_control_workflows_enabled is also true. A mode of 'none' causes the rule to fail. Preventive enforcement eliminates the window of exposure that exists with detective-only controls, preventing the fraud or privilege abuse scenario rather than merely detecting it post-hoc.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the RBAC or IGA platform configuration for the enforcement mode setting on the SoD policy engine.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A value of 'preventive', 'block', or 'hard_stop' confirms preventive mode. 'alert', 'report', or 'notify' indicates detective mode.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In SailPoint or Oracle Identity Governance, navigate to the SoD policy settings and check the policy action configured for violation responses.
how_to_obtain.navigation: SailPoint IdentityIQ → Governance → Policies → Select SoD Policy → Policy Action: 'Notify' (detective) vs 'Reject' (preventive). Oracle OIG → Compliance → Segregation of Duties → Policy Details → Response Action.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A 'Reject' or 'Prevent' action on provisioning requests confirms preventive mode; 'Notify' or 'Report' confirms detective mode.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Test the enforcement mode by attempting to assign two known conflicting roles to a test user account in a non-production environment and observe whether the system blocks or permits the assignment.
how_to_obtain.navigation: IAM Admin Console → User Management → Assign Roles → Attempt to assign Role A (e.g., PurchaseRequester) and then Role B (e.g., PurchaseApprover) to the same test user.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: System returning an error or blocking the second role assignment = preventive. System permitting assignment but generating an alert or violation report = detective. System doing neither = none.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the IGA platform to retrieve the enforcement action configured for each SoD policy.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' 'https://iga-platform.example.com/api/v1/policies/sod' | python3 -c "import json,sys; data=json.load(sys.stdin); [print(p['name'], '->', p.get('enforcement_action','unknown')) for p in data.get('policies',[])]"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each policy prints its enforcement action. Values of 'block'/'prevent'/'reject' = preventive; 'alert'/'notify'/'report' = detective; absent or 'none' = none.

option_description: The current number of users who are actively assigned to at least one pair of mutually exclusive roles as defined by the SoD policy. This is a real-time or point-in-time measurement of actual SoD policy violations in the live environment.
security_impact: This contextual evidence attribute informs the separation_of_duties_support rule's overall risk posture. While the rule evaluates structural controls, a non-zero sod_violation_count indicates that even defined constraints are not preventing accumulation of conflicting permissions—potentially due to legacy assignments, override approvals, or gaps in automated enforcement. High counts signal that preventive controls are either absent or being bypassed.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the IGA platform's violation report API to retrieve the current count of active SoD violations across all users.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' 'https://iga-platform.example.com/api/v1/violations/sod?status=active' | python3 -c "import json,sys; data=json.load(sys.stdin); print(f'Active SoD violations: {data.get(\"total_violations\", len(data.get(\"violations\", [])))}')"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Returns an integer count of active SoD violations. Target is 0.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For directory-integrated RBAC, query the directory to find users who are members of two or more defined conflicting groups simultaneously.
how_to_obtain.command:
python3 -c "
import ldap3
server = ldap3.Server('ldap://directory.example.com')
conn = ldap3.Connection(server, 'cn=admin,dc=example,dc=com', 'password', auto_bind=True)
conn.search('ou=users,dc=example,dc=com', '(&(memberOf=cn=PurchaseRequester,ou=groups,dc=example,dc=com)(memberOf=cn=PurchaseApprover,ou=groups,dc=example,dc=com))', attributes=['cn'])
print(f'SoD violations: {len(conn.entries)}')
"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Integer count of users in both conflicting groups. Zero confirms no active violations for that constraint pair.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Generate a SoD violation report from the identity governance dashboard to obtain the current violation count with user-level detail.
how_to_obtain.navigation: SailPoint IdentityIQ → Reports → Compliance → Segregation of Duties Violation Report → Run Report → View Total Violations count. Saviynt → Security Manager → Violations → SOD Violations Dashboard → Total Active Violations.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Report showing total violation count per policy and per user. Zero total active violations is the target state.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Parse recent access provisioning logs to count assignments that triggered SoD violation alerts or warnings, indicating violations that were permitted despite detection.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Count of SoD violation events logged. Zero is target. Any count indicates violations occurred during the log period and should be investigated.

option_description: Controls whether critical application workflows—such as financial transaction approval, privileged access grants, configuration changes, or bulk data exports—require a second user with a non-conflicting role to authorize the action before it is committed.
security_impact: This attribute enables the second branch of the separation_of_duties_support Rego rule: when sod_constraints_defined == true AND dual_control_workflows_enabled == true AND sod_enforcement_mode is 'preventive' or 'detective', the countermeasure activates. Dual-control provides a procedural SoD enforcement layer independent of role assignment controls, ensuring that even if SoD constraints have gaps, high-risk operations require multi-party authorization and cannot be completed by a single actor.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect workflow engine or BPM configuration files for approval step definitions on high-risk processes, verifying that a second approver role is required.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Workflow definitions containing an approval task requiring a different role from the initiator confirm dual-control is enabled for those processes.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the application's workflow or process management interface and inspect the approval chain configuration for critical workflows to verify a mandatory second-approver step exists.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Application Admin Panel → Workflow Configuration → Select high-risk workflow (e.g., 'Financial Disbursement') → Process Steps → Verify existence of 'Approval' step assigned to role different from 'Initiator'. ServiceNow: Process Automation → Workflow Editor → Select workflow → Inspect approval activities.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Workflow diagram or configuration showing a mandatory approval activity assigned to a role that excludes the initiating role confirms dual-control is enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the application owner or process owner to identify which workflows are classified as high-risk and whether each requires a second authorized party to complete.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Request the Business Process Controls documentation or Change Management procedures from the application owner, compliance team, or CISO office.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documentation confirming named high-risk workflows (financial approval, access grant, config change) each have a mandatory second-party authorization step with a non-overlapping role requirement.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the application or workflow API to retrieve workflow definitions and confirm approval steps are defined for critical process types.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' 'https://app.example.com/api/v1/workflows?type=critical' | python3 -c "import json,sys; data=json.load(sys.stdin); [print(w['name'], '-> approval_required:', any(s.get('type')=='approval' for s in w.get('steps',[]))) for w in data.get('workflows',[])]"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each critical workflow prints True for approval_required. Any False indicates dual-control is not enforced for that workflow.

option_description: Controls whether the application logs both granted and denied RBAC access decisions to an audit trail, capturing every authorization outcome for forensic and compliance purposes.
security_impact: The Rego policy rule `access_decision_logging` requires this attribute to be `true` as a prerequisite for the countermeasure to activate. Without it, there is no audit trail of who accessed what or who was blocked, making forensic investigation and compliance reporting impossible. This is a high-criticality attribute because silent authorization failures and undetected privilege abuse both stem from missing access decision logs.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the application's RBAC middleware or framework configuration file for an audit or logging toggle. Common frameworks store this in settings like `audit_logging: true`, `access_logging: enabled`, or `authorization_logging: on`.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A boolean flag or string value explicitly enabling access decision logging, e.g., `audit_logging: true` or `access_logging: enabled`.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search the codebase for authorization logging configuration flags using grep to locate where access decisions are recorded.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: File path and line showing the logging flag set to `true`, `enabled`, or equivalent. No results indicate logging is not configured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review recent application logs to verify that access decision events are actually being written. Search for both granted and denied authorization events in log output.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Log entries showing access decisions with timestamps. Absence of any authorization events confirms logging is disabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the application's observability or admin API to retrieve the current logging configuration if the framework exposes a management endpoint.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: `true` or `enabled` in the response body. A `null` or `false` response confirms logging is disabled.

option_description: Specifies which categories of access decisions are captured in logs — whether only denied attempts, only granted attempts, or both types are recorded in the audit trail.
security_impact: The Rego policy rule `access_decision_logging` checks that both `'granted'` and `'denied'` are present in this array. Logging only denied events misses insider threat scenarios where legitimate-looking granted accesses are abused. Logging only granted events misses brute-force enumeration attempts. Both values must be present for the countermeasure to satisfy policy requirements.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the authorization middleware or logging configuration for a list defining which decision outcomes trigger log writes. Look for arrays or comma-separated values specifying event types.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A list or array value such as `logged_decision_types: [granted, denied]` or `log_events: 'both'`.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search application source code for the authorization middleware hook to identify which decision outcomes invoke log write calls.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Code lines showing log calls for both `granted` and `denied` outcomes. Only one type present means incomplete logging coverage.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Sample recent audit logs and verify that both grant and deny events appear. Filter for each type separately to confirm both are present.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Non-zero counts for both `access_granted` and `access_denied`. A zero count for either confirms that decision type is not being logged.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the application security or DevOps team to confirm the intentional logging scope. Ask whether the logging policy captures all decision outcomes or is filtered to reduce log volume.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Verbal or documented confirmation that both granted and denied decisions are logged, with reference to the relevant configuration setting or code path.

option_description: Controls whether each access decision log entry captures the minimum required contextual fields: the user identity (who), the resource or endpoint accessed (what), the action attempted (how), and the role evaluated (under what authority).
security_impact: The Rego policy rule `access_decision_logging` requires this attribute to be `true` alongside enabled logging and both decision types. Log entries without user identity or resource context are forensically useless — investigators cannot determine which user accessed which resource or reconstruct an attack path. This is a medium-criticality attribute because incomplete log fields degrade the value of an otherwise enabled logging system.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Pull a sample of recent access decision log entries and manually inspect the fields present in each record to verify all required contextual data is included.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Structured log entries containing fields for `user_id` or `username`, `resource` or `endpoint`, `action`, `role`, and `decision`. Missing any of these fields indicates incomplete logging.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the structured logging schema or log formatter configuration to confirm which fields are included in authorization event records.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Schema definition listing fields `user`, `resource`, `action`, `role`, and `outcome` (or equivalents) in the audit log event structure.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search authorization middleware source code for the log write statement to confirm all required fields are included in the log payload construction.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Code lines showing all five fields (user, resource, action, role, decision) being passed into the log write call. Missing fields in the log payload confirm incomplete logging.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query a centralized SIEM or logging platform API to retrieve a recent authorization event and validate its field completeness programmatically.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' 'https://<siem-host>/api/v1/search?query=event_type:access_decision&limit=1' | jq '{user: .user_id, resource: .resource, action: .action, role: .role_evaluated, decision: .outcome}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All five fields returned with non-null values. Any `null` field in the output confirms that field is not being captured in logs.

option_description: Indicates whether a formal, documented process exists for creating new roles, including required approval gates, permission scoping guidelines, and least-privilege criteria that must be satisfied before a role is provisioned.
security_impact: The Rego policy rule `role_lifecycle_maintainability` requires this to be `true` as one of four conditions. Without a defined creation process, roles can be created ad hoc with excessive permissions, no documentation of intent, and no accountability trail. This enables permission sprawl and makes later audits impossible because there is no record of why a role was created or who approved its permission set.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request the access governance or identity management documentation from the security team. Look for a role management runbook, RBAC policy document, or ITSM change management procedure that covers new role requests.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Confluence / SharePoint: search for 'RBAC role creation process', 'access management procedure', or 'role provisioning runbook'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A documented procedure specifying the request form, approval chain (e.g., manager + security team sign-off), permission scoping requirements, and ticketing workflow for role creation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the ITSM or ticketing system (ServiceNow, Jira, etc.) for a role creation request template or change category to confirm a formal intake workflow exists.
how_to_obtain.navigation: ServiceNow: Service Catalog → Access Management → New Role Request. Jira: Project → Issue Types → 'RBAC Role Creation'. Check for required approval fields in the workflow.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A structured request form with mandatory fields for business justification, permissions requested, approver list, and least-privilege attestation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the RBAC system's administrative configuration for role provisioning workflow settings, which may reference approval workflows or policy enforcement on role creation.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A policy file or SOP document referencing approval requirements, permission constraints, and scoping criteria for new roles.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the repository for role definition files with commit history and PR review trails, which indirectly evidence a review process if roles are managed as code.
how_to_obtain.command: git log --oneline --follow -- roles/ | head -20 && git log --all --pretty=format:'%h %an %s' -- roles/*.yml | head -20
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Commit history showing role file changes with reviewer approvals in PR metadata, indicating roles go through a code-review-based creation process.

option_description: Indicates whether a formal process exists for retiring or decommissioning roles, covering user reassignment to alternative roles, role disablement or deletion steps, permission cleanup verification, and audit confirmation that no residual access remains.
security_impact: The Rego policy rule `role_lifecycle_maintainability` requires this to be `true`. Without a retirement process, obsolete roles accumulate in the system indefinitely, carrying permissions that no longer have a legitimate business purpose. This is a direct vector for permission accumulation — users may retain access through stale roles after job changes, and attackers who compromise such accounts gain access that should not exist.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request the role decommissioning or offboarding procedure from the IAM or security team. Verify the procedure covers user migration, role disablement timeline, permission cleanup confirmation, and audit sign-off steps.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Confluence / SharePoint: search for 'role decommissioning', 'RBAC retirement process', or 'role offboarding procedure'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A documented SOP with defined steps for: (1) identifying affected users, (2) migrating users to replacement roles, (3) disabling or deleting the retired role, (4) confirming no residual permissions remain.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the ITSM system to check for a role decommissioning request category or change template, confirming a formal intake path for role retirement exists.
how_to_obtain.navigation: ServiceNow: Service Catalog → Access Management → Role Decommission Request. Check for required fields covering user reassignment and cleanup confirmation.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A request template with mandatory fields for affected user list, replacement role assignment, and post-retirement audit confirmation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check administrative documentation or runbooks stored in the repository for role retirement guidance, including any automated scripts or playbooks that execute decommissioning steps.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A runbook or script documenting the ordered steps for retiring a role, with checkpoints for user migration and permission cleanup verification.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check whether recently deleted or disabled roles have an associated audit log entry or change record, providing evidence that a process was followed for past retirements.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Audit log entries showing role retirement events with actor identity, timestamps, and confirmation fields. Absence of any such entries may indicate ad hoc deletions without process.

option_description: Defines how frequently existing roles are formally reviewed for continued relevance, permission accuracy, and alignment with current organizational requirements, expressed as a frequency tier from continuous to never.
security_impact: The Rego policy rule `role_lifecycle_maintainability` requires this value to be one of `continuous`, `quarterly`, `semi_annually`, or `annually`. Values of `ad_hoc` or `never` fail the policy. Infrequent reviews allow permission drift to accumulate undetected — roles may retain permissions from deprecated features, former employees, or superseded job functions. The shorter the review cycle, the faster drift is caught and remediated.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request the access governance policy or access review schedule from the security or compliance team. Look for a defined recertification cadence tied to role entitlement reviews.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Confluence / SharePoint: search for 'access review schedule', 'role recertification policy', or 'entitlement review calendar'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A policy document specifying the review frequency (e.g., quarterly, semi-annually) with assigned owners and scheduled review dates.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the identity governance platform (SailPoint, Saviynt, Okta Governance, etc.) for configured access review campaign schedules targeting role entitlements.
how_to_obtain.navigation: SailPoint IdentityNow: Admin → Access Reviews → Campaigns → filter by 'Role Review'. Saviynt: Access Governance → Campaigns → Schedule. Check campaign recurrence settings.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An active campaign schedule showing role review recurrence (e.g., every 90 days). No active campaigns or a 'manual' trigger confirms `ad_hoc` or `never` status.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review governance platform configuration files or policy definitions for scheduled review job configurations.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A schedule definition specifying the review interval, such as `review_frequency: quarterly` or a cron expression equivalent to the desired cadence.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the identity governance platform API or database to retrieve the configured review campaign schedule for roles.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' 'https://<iga-host>/api/v1/campaigns?type=role_review' | jq '[.items[] | {name: .name, frequency: .schedule.frequency, last_run: .lastRun, next_run: .nextRun}]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Campaign objects with `frequency` set to a value like `quarterly` or `semi_annually` and a `nextRun` date confirming active scheduling.

option_description: Indicates whether the RBAC system contains roles that have zero current user assignments and lack either a documented business purpose or a scheduled deletion plan, representing lifecycle management gaps.
security_impact: The Rego policy rule `role_lifecycle_maintainability` requires this to be `false` for the countermeasure to activate. Orphaned roles represent unmanaged permission sets that could be exploited if an attacker gains the ability to assign roles — they represent 'ready-made' privilege escalation paths. They also inflate the attack surface for authorization bypass and indicate the role lifecycle process is not being followed.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the application's RBAC system or identity platform API to retrieve all roles and filter for those with zero user assignments, then cross-reference against a role registry.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <admin_token>' 'https://<app-host>/api/v1/roles?include_user_count=true' | jq '[.roles[] | select(.user_count == 0) | {role_id: .id, name: .name, created_at: .created_at}]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An empty array `[]` indicates no orphaned roles. Any roles listed with `user_count: 0` are candidates for orphan status and require documentation review.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the application database directly to identify roles with no active user-role assignments.
how_to_obtain.command: psql -U dbadmin -d appdb -c "SELECT r.id, r.name, r.created_at FROM roles r LEFT JOIN user_roles ur ON r.id = ur.role_id WHERE ur.role_id IS NULL ORDER BY r.created_at DESC;"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Zero rows returned indicates no orphaned roles. Any rows returned list role names and creation dates for roles with no assigned users.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the RBAC administration console to view all roles with their member counts and identify any with zero members lacking a documented owner or retirement plan.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Application Admin Panel → Access Management → Roles → Sort by 'Members' ascending. Alternatively: Okta Admin → Directory → Groups → filter by 'No Members'. SailPoint: Role Management → filter by 'Member Count: 0'.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Role list sorted by member count showing all zero-member roles. Each should be cross-referenced against a role registry; undocumented zero-member roles are orphans.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request the role registry or role inventory document from the IAM team and compare documented roles against the active role list in the RBAC system to identify undocumented entries.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A role registry listing all roles with their business owner, purpose, and status. Roles present in the system but absent from the registry confirm orphaned role presence.

option_description: Indicates whether the application evaluates all RBAC permission decisions at a single, dedicated enforcement layer — such as an authorization middleware, API gateway policy engine, or dedicated policy decision point (e.g., OPA, Casbin) — rather than implementing permission checks individually within each controller or feature module.
security_impact: The Rego policy rule `centralized_policy_enforcement` requires this attribute to be `true` alongside full enforcement coverage scope and no per-feature permission logic. Decentralized permission checks are highly prone to inconsistency — a missed check in one controller creates an authorization bypass for that resource. Centralized enforcement guarantees uniform policy application and enables single-point policy updates without modifying individual feature code.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the application's middleware stack or filter chain configuration to identify whether a single authorization component intercepts all requests before they reach business logic handlers.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A middleware registration showing an authorization or RBAC enforcement component applied globally (e.g., `app.use(authorizationMiddleware)` in Express, or `AddAuthorization()` in ASP.NET Core applied before route handling).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search the codebase for permission check calls (e.g., `hasPermission`, `authorize`, `checkRole`) to determine whether they are centralized in middleware or scattered across individual controllers and service files.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A count of zero (or near-zero) indicates all permission checks are centralized. A high count of matches outside middleware/policy files confirms scattered per-feature permission logic.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for a policy engine configuration file (OPA, Casbin, AWS Cedar, etc.) that defines centralized authorization rules, confirming a dedicated policy decision point is in use.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A policy engine configuration file defining RBAC rules centrally. Its presence confirms a dedicated enforcement point; its absence suggests inline permission logic.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the API gateway configuration (Kong, AWS API Gateway, Nginx with auth plugins, Envoy with OPA) to confirm authorization policies are applied at the gateway layer before requests reach upstream services.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Kong Admin: Services → select service → Plugins → check for 'RBAC', 'OPA', or 'JWT' authorization plugins applied globally. AWS API Gateway: Authorizers → check for Lambda or Cognito authorizer applied to all methods. Envoy: check ext_authz filter in listener config.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A globally applied authorization plugin or authorizer configuration on the gateway, confirming centralized enforcement. No gateway-level authorization plugin indicates enforcement is delegated to individual services.

option_description: Controls whether individual application modules or feature controllers contain their own inline permission checks rather than delegating all authorization decisions to a centralized enforcement point. When true, permission logic is fragmented across the codebase.
security_impact: The Rego rule `centralized_policy_enforcement` requires this value to be false. Fragmented per-feature permission logic creates inconsistent enforcement, making it easy for developers to forget authorization checks in new features, miss edge cases, or apply subtly different rules. Centralized enforcement eliminates these gaps by ensuring every request passes through a single authoritative gate before reaching business logic.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Grep the codebase for common permission/role-checking patterns in non-authorization module files (e.g., controllers, services, route handlers) to detect inline authorization logic outside the central enforcement layer.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No output (exit 0) indicates no per-feature permission logic. Any matching lines identify files where inline checks exist outside the authorization module.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search for decorator-based or annotation-based authorization hints embedded in controller or service files to find per-feature permission checks in frameworks like Spring, NestJS, or Django.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Results in controller/service directories (outside a dedicated auth module) confirm per-feature permission logic is present and should be flagged true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the application's architecture documentation or conduct a developer interview to determine whether the team uses a single authorization middleware/service or allows feature teams to add their own permission checks.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documentation or developer confirmation that all authorization is routed through one module/middleware indicates false; acknowledgment of feature-level checks indicates true.

typical_values: true (fragmented codebases without enforced architecture standards)
false (mature applications with gateway or middleware-enforced RBAC)

option_description: Defines the breadth of application routes, modules, and endpoints that are subject to the centralized RBAC enforcement point. 'full' means all routes pass through centralized authorization, 'partial' means only some routes are covered, and 'none' means no centralized enforcement exists.
security_impact: The Rego rule `centralized_policy_enforcement` requires this value to be 'full'. Any partial or no coverage leaves application endpoints unprotected, allowing unauthenticated or under-privileged users to access functions by targeting uncovered routes. Partial coverage is particularly dangerous because developers may incorrectly assume all routes are protected.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the application's middleware registration or route configuration file to determine whether the authorization middleware is applied globally (all routes) or selectively (specific route groups).
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Global middleware registration (e.g., `app.use(authMiddleware)` before all routes, or `@UseGuards` at module root) indicates 'full'. Route-specific registration indicates 'partial'. Absence of any authorization middleware registration indicates 'none'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Enumerate all registered routes and cross-reference them against the routes that have the authorization middleware/guard applied, identifying any unprotected routes.
how_to_obtain.command: npx ts-node -e "const app = require('./src/app'); console.log(app._router.stack.filter(r => r.route).map(r => ({path: r.route.path, methods: Object.keys(r.route.methods), hasAuth: r.route.stack.some(l => l.name.includes('auth') || l.name.includes('guard'))})))" 2>/dev/null || python manage.py show_urls 2>/dev/null | head -50
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All routes showing auth middleware applied = 'full'. Some routes without auth = 'partial'. No routes with auth = 'none'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the application framework's admin or route inspection panel (if available), or use API gateway configuration UI to review which route groups have authorization policies attached.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS API Gateway Console → APIs → [Your API] → Authorizers → Check which routes have an authorizer assigned | Kong Manager → Routes → Review plugins per route for authentication plugins
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All routes showing an authorizer/policy = 'full'. Missing authorizers on some routes = 'partial'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Send unauthenticated HTTP requests to a sample of application endpoints to verify whether unauthorized access is rejected across all routes or only some.
how_to_obtain.command: for endpoint in /api/users /api/admin /api/reports /api/health /api/export; do echo -n "$endpoint: "; curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" -X GET http://localhost:8080$endpoint; echo; done
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All non-public endpoints returning 401 or 403 for unauthenticated requests indicates 'full'. Mixed results (some 200, some 401) indicate 'partial'.

typical_values: partial (most common - teams add auth incrementally)

option_description: Indicates whether the application has explicitly defined distinct roles (such as 'admin', 'data-exporter', or 'auditor') that are required to perform sensitive or destructive operations including deletion, bulk export, and administrative configuration changes.
security_impact: The Rego rule `privileged_action_prevention_coverage` requires this to be true. Without defined privileged roles, the RBAC model has no mechanism to gate high-risk operations — all authenticated users may have implicit access to destructive functions. Explicit role definitions create the access boundary that limits blast radius if a standard account is compromised.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the application's role definition configuration files, IAM policy documents, or seeding scripts to confirm named privileged roles exist with scoped sensitive permissions.
how_to_obtain.command: cat ./config/roles.yml 2>/dev/null || cat ./src/rbac/roles.ts 2>/dev/null || cat ./db/seeds/roles.rb 2>/dev/null || find . -name 'roles*' -o -name 'permissions*' | head -10 | xargs cat
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Role definitions containing entries like 'admin', 'superuser', 'data-exporter', 'auditor' with explicit permission assignments to delete/export/configure actions confirm true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the application's roles management API endpoint to retrieve all defined roles and inspect whether privileged roles with sensitive operation permissions exist.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response listing roles including at least one privileged role (e.g., admin, superadmin) with permissions referencing delete, export, or admin-config actions confirms true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the application's role management section in the admin console to view all defined roles and their assigned permissions.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Admin Console → Settings → Roles & Permissions → View All Roles → Review each role for sensitive operation permissions (delete, export, admin-config)
how_to_obtain.expected_output: At least one role visible with explicit destructive/sensitive operation permissions confirms true. Only a single default role or no sensitive-action permissions confirms false.

typical_values: true (applications with mature RBAC and separated admin functions)
false (simple applications using single-role or flat permission models)

option_description: Measures whether role-based authorization checks are applied to all sensitive and destructive operations — specifically delete actions, bulk data exports, and administrative configuration changes. 'full' means every such operation requires an explicit role check, 'partial' means only some operations are protected, and 'none' means no role checks exist on sensitive operations.
security_impact: The Rego rule `privileged_action_prevention_coverage` requires this to be 'full'. Partial enforcement is particularly dangerous because it gives a false sense of security — attackers who discover unprotected sensitive endpoints can perform destructive actions even if they cannot access other privileged areas. Full enforcement ensures consistent protection across all high-risk operations.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Enumerate all route handlers or controller methods implementing delete, export, or admin-config operations, then check each for the presence of a role/permission guard before execution.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each matched operation should have a corresponding authorization check (guard, decorator, middleware call) immediately before or wrapping it. Unguarded sensitive operations confirm 'partial' or 'none'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt sensitive operations (delete, export) using a standard (non-privileged) user token and verify whether all operations return 403 Forbidden.
how_to_obtain.command: STANDARD_TOKEN=$(curl -s -X POST https://app.example.com/api/auth/login -d '{"user":"standard@example.com","password":"password"}' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' | jq -r '.token'); for op in 'DELETE /api/resources/1' 'GET /api/export/users' 'POST /api/admin/config'; do method=$(echo $op | cut -d' ' -f1); path=$(echo $op | cut -d' ' -f2); echo -n "$method $path: "; curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" -X $method -H "Authorization: Bearer $STANDARD_TOKEN" https://app.example.com$path; echo; done
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All sensitive operations returning 403 for standard user token = 'full'. Mixed results (some 200, some 403) = 'partial'. All returning 200 = 'none'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the security requirements documentation or threat model to identify all operations classified as sensitive or destructive, then audit each against the RBAC configuration to determine coverage.
